record_identity.title: Anthropic reported Moonshot and DeepSeek routed customer conversations through Claude for distillation

incident_identity.historical_event_name: 2026 Moonshot and DeepSeek customer-conversation routing and distillation campaigns
incident_identity.date_basis: Anthropic's September 2026 threat-intelligence report states that Moonshot activity attributable to the campaign occurred between May and July 2026 and that the DeepSeek campaign included more than 12.1 million exchanges over 14 days in July 2026. The range is an occurrence envelope rather than an assertion of continuous activity.

summary: Anthropic reported that Moonshot AI and DeepSeek silently routed real customer requests through Claude and used resulting exchanges or reasoning traces in model-distillation and training workflows. Anthropic states that Moonshot users believed they were using Kimi while receiving Claude responses, and that DeepSeek similarly relayed selected customer requests to Claude without informing customers. Anthropic reported more than 23 million Moonshot-attributable exchanges between May and July 2026 and more than 12.1 million DeepSeek-attributable exchanges over 14 days in July, with some routed material containing sensitive customer or organisational information. Public reporting does not identify individual affected users or establish their jurisdictions, and the provider attribution is not treated as an adjudication of legal liability. Anthropic also described cross-session replay of thinking signatures to obtain reasoning traces and subsequent disruption of the campaigns.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Anthropic's September 2026 threat-intelligence report directly describes separate Moonshot and DeepSeek campaigns. For Moonshot, Anthropic states that customer requests were silently forwarded to Claude rather than processed by Kimi, Claude responses were shown to users, at least some exchanges were captured and saved, and extracted Claude reasoning traces were used for model training. For DeepSeek, Anthropic states that selected user requests were silently relayed to Claude and that the resulting reasoning traces were extracted for downstream distillation. Anthropic reports more than 23 million exchanges attributable to Moonshot between May and July 2026 and more than 12.1 million exchanges attributable to DeepSeek over 14 days in July. Reuters, The Wall Street Journal and the South China Morning Post independently report Anthropic's findings concerning live customer-query routing and sensitive information. The available public evidence does not identify individual affected users or establish their jurisdictions, and VIGIL does not treat Anthropic's provider attribution as an independently adjudicated legal finding. The later provider report describes cross-session replay and defensive changes. It does not identify each customer’s notice, jurisdiction or contractual processing basis. The earlier distillation disclosure concerns a separate reporting period.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The reported conduct separates into three mechanisms. Customer requests were silently relayed from the selected service to Claude, changing the processing principal and creating an authority-scope boundary whose contractual or consent basis is not public. The customer-facing responses were also represented as coming from the selected service/model even though Anthropic reports Claude generated them, creating a source-attribution failure. Separately, saved exchanges and extracted reasoning traces were used for training/distillation, a materially different secondary purpose, and the campaign scale supports Industrial-Scale Capability Extraction. VIGIL preserves Anthropic's attribution as provider-reported evidence rather than an independent legal finding. Provider-attributed source misrepresentation and secondary-purpose/cumulative extraction failures remain distinct from unresolved cross-provider customer authority and consequential trust-cue effects. OECD AI awareness does not require identification of the exact model; users knew they interacted with an AI service, while provider substitution remains a separate taxonomy issue. The reported privacy and secondary-use outcome is Not aligned. Awareness of interacting with AI is Aligned for the reported Kimi users. Backend disclosure, training-data verification, storage and red-team coverage remain separate Boundary assessments. The reported silent forwarding to Claude materially engages a recipient boundary for customer requests. The public report does not establish the request-specific confidentiality restrictions and permitted processors. Neither an unauthorised protected disclosure nor verified authorised handling can be concluded for those customer requests.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The occurrence demonstrates that model routing is not merely infrastructure metadata. A user-facing model identity can conceal a materially different processing chain in which user content crosses providers and becomes input to model development. Governance therefore needs purpose-bound authority, routing provenance and user-facing disclosure sufficient to distinguish which model actually processed information, whether information was relayed to another provider, and whether it entered a training or distillation pathway. The case also shows that secondary-purpose data use and industrial-scale model extraction can co-occur without being collapsed into one mechanism.
assessment_boundaries: The occurrence is reported and attributed by Anthropic; VIGIL does not independently adjudicate the named firms' legal liability or contractual breach.
Reuters, The Wall Street Journal and the South China Morning Post independently report Anthropic's findings but do not independently reproduce Anthropic's underlying traffic telemetry.
VIGIL does not assert that Australian personal information was among the routed conversations; the reviewed public evidence does not identify affected users by nationality or residence.
Sensitive-data examples are attributed only where Anthropic allocates them to a named campaign; broad reporting about sensitive routed data is not redistributed between firms without source support.

Secondary-Purpose Authority Transposition classifies the reported repurposing of service-delivery data into a materially different model-development purpose; it does not imply that all model routing or all distillation is unauthorised.

Industrial-Scale Unauthorised Capability Extraction classifies the reported industrial-scale capability-extraction campaign; legitimate distillation undertaken with valid authority remains outside the class.
The model-substitution and disclosure issue is recorded as a governance finding but is not assigned an additional taxonomy class absent a cleaner current fit.

Anthropic reports that customers believed they were receiving responses from Kimi or DeepSeek while Claude actually generated the responses, materially misrepresenting the source role of the customer-facing output. Anthropic reports repeated, concealed campaigns at tens of millions of exchanges in which Claude outputs and reasoning traces were harvested for downstream model training, satisfying the industrial-scale capability-extraction mechanism. Customer requests were reportedly relayed from the service users selected to Claude, changing the processing principal and path; the public record does not expose whether the customer authority basis validly covered that cross-provider processing. Silent routing concealed the provider of responses and downstream training purpose from customers, but a changed consequential customer choice caused by that trust cue is not shown. The reported silent forwarding to Claude materially engages a recipient boundary for customer requests. The public report does not establish the request-specific confidentiality restrictions and permitted processors. Neither an unauthorised protected disclosure nor verified authorised handling can be concluded for those customer requests.
